entry.evidence: The objective of this paper is to present a new forecast-oriented coupled ocean–atmosphere system.

steps.action: The authors frame the gap: few kilometre-scale coupled systems are forecast-oriented or operational, and operational regional systems in western Europe do not represent air–sea interactions; they argue a dedicated coupled prediction system is needed.
steps.quote: developing a dedicated ocean–atmosphere coupled prediction system now appears essential to improve the high-resolution regional forecasts on both sides

steps.action: The starting point is the AROME–NEMO coupled system of Rainaud et al. (2017) and Lebeaupin Brossier et al. (2017), and the OASIS interface in SurfEx (Voldoire et al. 2017); co-authors are on these works, so the steps are inherited and cited, not performed here.
steps.quote: [...] coupled system is an extension and update of the ocean–atmosphere coupled system developed by

steps.action: The authors build the new system. They extend the NEMO IBI configuration into eNEATL36 (1/36°, covering the Tyrrhenian Sea) and define a 2.5 km AROME domain. They add the full current-feedback effect to the AROME turbulence scheme and implement surface-pressure exchange through OASIS3-MCT.
steps.quote: the full current-feedback (CFB) effect has been added in the turbulent scheme of AROME

steps.action: The authors select the 12–19 October 2018 period as the test case: storm Callum, ex-hurricanes Leslie and Michael, and the Aude heavy-precipitation event. They chose it because it is expected to foster large air–sea interactions and coupling sensitivity.
steps.quote: The sensitivity of this coupled system is carried out through 7 d simulations of a case study from 12 to 19 October 2018.

steps.action: The authors describe the observed event chronology and intensities (gusts, rainfall totals, the Aude 342 mm maximum) taken from Met Office, NHC, Météo-France and published studies (Kendon et al., Caumont et al., Mandement and Caumont).
steps.quote: The Météo-France quantitative precipitation estimation gives a maximum 24 h accumulated rainfall total of 342 mm close to Trèbes

steps.action: The authors design four experiments: coupled OA; ARO, AROME with persistent SST and no currents, close to operational AROME-IFS; OCE-ifs, NEMO forced by IFS, close to operational IBI; and intermediate OCE-aro, NEMO forced by ARO bulk variables. The design separates the coupling effect from the forcing-model effect.
steps.quote: permits as to disentangle the ocean–atmosphere coupling effect on the ocean forecast from the impact of the atmospheric forcing change

steps.action: The authors run the 7 d simulations and describe the OA SST evolution: storm-induced cooling of up to 2.5 °C from vertical mixing, and domain-mean cooling of 0.6 °C.
steps.quote: the signatures of the Callum, Leslie and Mickael storms are visible

steps.action: The authors compare the +168 h SST of all experiments with L3S satellite SST interpolated on the observation grid (Fig. 4, Table 3). Persistent-SST ARO has a +0.38 °C mean bias; OA and OCE-aro are near −0.1/−0.06 °C, with overly strong Celtic Sea cooling; OCE-ifs is closest (−0.01 °C).
steps.quote: the simulated SST values are close to the observed SST

steps.action: The authors check the SST evolution against an independent in situ data set: 33 Coriolis drifting buoys with near-complete hourly series, summarized in a Taylor diagram. ARO drifts furthest; the other three show a mean bias of about 0.04 °C and a correlation of about 0.4.
steps.quote: the OA, OCE-aro and OCE-ifs simulations thus accurately reproduce the mean gradient, mesoscale structures and evolution of SST

steps.action: In four 50 km boxes, the authors compare SST time series across experiments. Changing the forcing model from IFS to AROME changes the surface ocean response more than interactive coupling does; coupling adds cooling after about 3 days; persistent SST errs by more than 0.5 °C in 2 d.
steps.quote: the effect of changing the atmospheric model to force NEMO is larger than the effect of an interactive coupling on the simulated surface fields

steps.action: The authors propose a mechanism for the coupled cooling enhancement: a positive feedback in which surface cooling lowers 2 m humidity, which enhances evaporation and amplifies cooling. The supporting heat-flux diagnostics are partly 'not shown'.
steps.quote: the coupled simulation represents an amplification loop, as the 2 m specific humidity is progressively lower in OA

steps.action: The authors compare SSS, SSH, surface currents and vertical temperature/MLD profiles across experiments in the four boxes. Forcing differences (IFS vs AROME) dominate; coupling effects on SSS, SSH and SSC are small; Callum deepens the Celtic Sea MLD by up to 65 m.
steps.quote: differences are larger when comparing OCE-ifs to OA than when comparing OA and OCE-aro

steps.action: The authors check mixed-layer temperature (about 13 m) of OCE-ifs and OCE-aro against independent CORA 5.2 in situ profiles (Argo, CTD, moorings, gliders) by RMSE. Mean skill is similar (OCE-ifs slightly better), with local improvements under AROME forcing along the Cornwall coast.
steps.quote: OCE-ifs and OCE-aro have been compared to the available in situ profile measurements

steps.action: From pairwise MLD differences (Fig. 9, Fig. 10), the authors keep the claim that the forcing-model change drives most near-surface ocean changes and that coupling only accentuates them.
steps.quote: the effect of the change in atmospheric forcing is responsible for the main signature in changes in the near-surface oceanic structure

steps.action: The authors compare 10 m wind from OA, ARO and IFS with Coriolis mooring observations (Fig. 11, Fig. 12). OA and ARO overestimate strong winds (mean bias 1.3 m/s, correlation 0.36), and IFS scores better at moorings. OA–ARO differences reach ±5 m/s along Callum and more than 100% locally after 3–6 days.
steps.quote: shows that OA and ARO overestimate wind speed at that time

steps.action: The authors attribute the wind-speed bias to a known systematic AROME bias reported by Rainaud et al. (2016) and Léger et al. (2016), and leave its origin out of scope instead of revising the coupled system.
steps.quote: Further investigation would be needed to understand the origin of such a systematic bias

steps.action: The authors compare simulated rainfall with observations and between OA and ARO. The Aude maximum (300 mm in 1 d) is reproduced in magnitude but shifted about 100 km east. Coupling changes local totals by more than 100% while the domain mean changes by less than 0.5%. Shifted convergence lines are taken as confirming earlier studies.
steps.quote: the simulated accumulated precipitation reaches 300 mm in 1 d as observed but is located about 100 km to the east of the observed one

steps.action: The authors conclude that the coupled system slightly changes the atmospheric forecast on average with strong local differences, and improves the SST forecast relative to the uncoupled systems.
steps.quote: significantly improves the sea surface temperature forecast (with a bias reduction of 30 %)

steps.action: The authors characterize the system's computational cost on the Belenos supercomputer (Appendix A, Table A1): OA costs about 20% more CPU than ARO, with similar elapsed time; they report OASIS overhead as negligible and present this as affordability.
steps.quote: indicating that the effect of the OASIS coupler is negligible for this coupled system

end.claim: The new 2.5 km AROME–NEMO coupled system reproduces SST and 10 m wind for the October 2018 storms. It improves the SST forecast against the uncoupled systems (with a wind overestimation) at about 20% extra CPU cost, and its ocean sensitivity comes mainly from the forcing-model change rather than from interactive coupling.

decisive_move.sentence: Without building the extended eNEATL36/AROME-Mercator coupled configuration (with full current feedback and pressure exchange), none of the characterization or sensitivity claims would exist.

gates.evidence: The case was chosen because it is 'known to foster large air–sea interactions' (§3.1 ¶6); the four-experiment design was set to disentangle coupling from forcing (§3.2 ¶4), but no hypothesis with predicted outcomes directed data acquisition. The claim faced satellite SST, drifting-buoy, CORA and mooring comparisons that could have shown poor skill (§4.1.1 ¶2–3, §4.2.1 ¶4), with no stated acceptance thresholds. Nothing was reported fixed before results were seen.

imports.item: Belenos supercomputer and the Vortex/Olive Python-based workflow framework used to run and cost the simulations

novelty_claims.quote: The objective of this paper is to present a new forecast-oriented coupled ocean–atmosphere system.
the full current-feedback (CFB) effect has been added in the turbulent scheme of AROME
the possibility of exchanging atmospheric surface pressure was implemented in this study
This work concretes our common first stage towards high-resolution ocean–atmosphere coupling for both oceanic and atmospheric forecasts.

limits:
Single 7 d case, one deterministic run per configuration: no ensemble, no repeated cases, and no significance testing of OA–ARO differences, so coupling impacts on wind and rainfall are not separated from chaotic divergence (inference). AROME runs without data assimilation, and forecast ranges (+66 to +90 h for the Aude event) exceed operational ranges. Several mechanism diagnostics are 'not shown' (non-solar heat flux, evaporation, precipitation effect on SSS).

The headline '30% SST bias reduction' (§5 ¶4) is not traceable to a stated computation; Table 3 mean biases (0.38 vs −0.10 °C) do not obviously give 30% (inference).

Sub-claims and their statuses:
- Forecast-model change dominates over coupling in the ocean response: best_explanation among the three configurations.
- Cooling–evaporation positive feedback under coupling: best_explanation, partly undocumented.
- Coupling shifts heavy-rain location via convergence: best_explanation, stated as confirming Rainaud et al. 2017 and Meroni et al. 2018.
- Computational affordability: capability_characterized for one node layout, not optimized.

Composition is coded capability_first because the walk is build-then-characterize with no rival tested before the capability. There is no 'establish the phenomenon until it repeats' phase, so the fit is partial.

No review file or discussion was supplied, although the paper records a discussion stage and two referees; changes made in review are unknown.

disagreements.target: current operational regional forecasting systems in western Europe (constant/persistent SST in NWP; IFS-forced ocean forecasts)
disagreements.support: ARO, with persistent SST as in operational AROME, has the largest SST bias (+0.38 °C, growing in time); coupling changes wind and rainfall location locally; the forcing-model change strongly alters the ocean forecast.
disagreements.quote: which is not the case in current operational regional forecasting systems used [...]

disagreements.target: former AROME–NEMO couplings (Rainaud et al. 2017; Lebeaupin Brossier et al. 2017; Sauvage et al. 2021)
disagreements.support: The paper adds the second current-feedback pathway (in the turbulence scheme), following Renault et al. (2019a), which the earlier couplings lacked; its effect is not separately evaluated.
disagreements.quote: Only the first effect was included in the former AROME–NEMO couplings

disagreements.target: Rainaud et al. (2017), Lebeaupin Brossier et al. (2017) and Arnold et al. (2021) coupling set-ups
disagreements.support: Atmospheric surface pressure is exchanged interactively for the inverse barometer approximation, unlike in those set-ups; no separate test of its effect is reported.
disagreements.quote: the possibility of exchanging atmospheric surface pressure was implemented in this study
